context: supply chain · shop drawings → fabrication → coating → delivery by erection sequence → erection

brief.intro: New to this project type? A steel-structure package — an industrial building, a pipe rack, a hangar, a stadium roof — is a supply chain more than a site job. The engineer's design is turned into shop drawings that show every piece and every bolt hole; the fabricator orders the steel, cuts, drills and welds it into members, blasts and paints or galvanises them, and trucks them to site in exactly the order the erector needs. On site the members are sorted, lifted, bolted, plumbed and tightened; then decking, cladding and fire protection follow. Erection is fast and very visible, so people watch it — but the schedule is decided earlier: by approval of the shop drawings, by steel procurement, and by the fabrication shop's throughput. And erection cannot start until the foundations and anchor bolts are finished, surveyed and handed over.

the order placed with the steel mill or stockist for raw sections and plates.
the unique number stamped on each member, matching the erection drawing.
the planned order of lifting, which the fabrication and delivery order must follow.

must_get_right: Shop-drawing approval is the first critical activity: nothing can be ordered or cut until drawings are approved, and late design changes go straight to the critical path.
Fabricate and deliver in erection sequence. Steel made in the wrong order fills the laydown area with pieces that cannot be lifted while the crane waits for the ones it needs.
Foundations and anchor bolts must be complete, surveyed and handed over before the first lift — agree that handover date with the civil contractor and protect it.
Plan the cranes with the erection sequence: crane positions, reach and the heaviest lift decide the method and the durations.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by erection zone, and every zone carries the same chain — drawings, material, fabrication, coating, delivery, erection — so the supply chain can be read zone by zone.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Shop calendar for fabrication (often two shifts); standard site calendar for erection with wind-day allowances for lifting.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Per zone: shop drawings → approval → material → fabrication → inspection → coating → delivery → erection → alignment → bolting → decking and cladding → fire protection. Zones follow each other in erection sequence; foundations with surveyed anchor bolts must precede erection in each zone. The critical path runs through shop-drawing approval and fabrication of the first zones, then through the crane sequence.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The structural design is frozen when detailing starts; approvals are returned within the agreed period; foundations are handed over in erection sequence; laydown space and crane access are available.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Anchor bolts before foundations; bolts before erection

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Shop capacity (tonnes per week); transport dimensions of large pieces; crane reach and capacity; wind limits for lifting; limited laydown area.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: design changes after detailing, slow approvals, steel delivery, fabrication errors found at site, anchor-bolt misalignment, and wind. Contingency is held before the handover of the structure to the following trades.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by erection zone; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the fabrication shop and the erection gangs — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
